articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for June 2026
body: The OCC released its June 2026 enforcement actions covering consent orders, formal agreements, and civil money penalties against federally regulated banks. The monthly release is the primary mechanism through which the OCC publicizes supervisory actions taken during the prior month.

articles.headline: OCC Releases May 2026 Enforcement Actions — Three Terminations, AI Model Risk Remains Top Priority
body: The OCC released its May 2026 enforcement actions, including termination of formal agreements with Axiom Bank and Cenlar Federal Savings Bank. The OCC confirmed AI model risk governance remains its top examination priority for 2026.
Updated model risk management guidance was issued jointly with the Federal Reserve and FDIC on April 17, 2026.

articles.headline: OCC Consent Order Against Federal Savings Bank Chicago — $10.8B in VA Loans, Deceptive Marketing
body: The OCC issued a consent order against The Federal Savings Bank of Chicago for deceptive marketing of VA-backed cash-out refinance loans to military service members between 2022 and 2024. The bank originated $10.8 billion in loans covering 30,361 transactions.
This is the bank's second consent order in five years. The board must engage an independent restitution consultant within 90 days.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for April 2026
body: The OCC released its April 2026 enforcement actions, including consent orders, formal agreements, orders of prohibition, and civil money penalties against nationally chartered banks and affiliated individuals.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for March 2026
body: The OCC released its March 2026 enforcement actions, including orders of prohibition against former bank employees and terminations of prior enforcement actions for several institutions that achieved satisfactory compliance.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Proposed Rulemaking to Implement GENIUS Act on Stablecoin Regulation
body: The OCC issued a proposed rulemaking to implement the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, setting regulations for permitted payment stablecoin issuers under OCC jurisdiction.
The proposed rule covers custody activities by OCC-supervised entities, establishing for the first time a comprehensive federal framework for stablecoin issuance.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for January 2026
body: The OCC released its January 2026 enforcement actions, including orders of prohibition against former bank employees and civil money penalties. The OCC also announced terminations of formal agreements for institutions demonstrating sustained compliance improvements.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2025

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for September 2025

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for August 2025
body: The OCC released its August 2025 enforcement actions covering consent orders, formal agreements, and civil money penalties. The release reflects ongoing OCC supervisory priorities including interest rate risk, liquidity management, and BSA/AML compliance.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for July 2025
body: The OCC released its July 2025 enforcement actions against national banks and federal savings associations, covering consent orders for unsafe or unsound banking practices and individual prohibition orders.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for June 2025

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for May 2025 — Cease and Desist Orders Against Two National Banks
body: The OCC released its May 2025 enforcement actions, including cease and desist orders against Eastern National Bank of Miami for unsafe practices related to strategic and capital planning, and against EH National Bank of Beverly Hills for deficiencies in management and board supervision.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for April 2025
body: The OCC released its April 2025 enforcement actions, including orders of prohibition against former JPMorgan Chase employees for embezzlement and misappropriation, and a former TD Bank employee for fraudulently obtaining PPP loan proceeds.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for March 2025 — Cease and Desist Order Against 42 North Private Bank
body: The OCC released its March 2025 enforcement actions, including a cease and desist order against 42 North Private Bank for unsafe or unsound practices related to interest rate risk, strategic planning, capital, liquidity, and earnings management.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for February 2025 — Formal Agreement with Dearborn Federal Savings Bank
body: The OCC released its February 2025 enforcement actions, including a formal agreement with Dearborn Federal Savings Bank for unsafe or unsound practices related to compliance management, fair lending risk management, insider activities, and compensation practices.

articles.headline: OCC Announces January 2025 Enforcement Actions — Bank of America Cease and Desist for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The OCC announced January 2025 enforcement actions including a cease and desist order against Bank of America, N.A. for violations related to its BSA/AML and sanctions compliance programs. A $1.5 million civil money penalty was assessed against Paul McLinko, former Executive Audit Director at Wells Fargo, for compliance failures.
The OCC also announced updates to its enforcement action search tool to improve public access to supervisory action records.

articles.headline: Additions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 7 entities to the Entity List, under the destinations of Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These entities have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.
